1.explanation: All of the built-in drawing routines live in Draw.js: that file exports the geometryFunction implementations for type ‘Circle’, for createRegularPolygon (square, triangle, etc.), and createBox.  Those functions all use simple planar trigonometry (dx, dy, Math.cos/sin, flat Euclidean distance) and never check the view’s useGeographic flag or use geodesic math.  Circle.js in turn implements the Circle geometry class itself in planar coordinates.  Because neither Draw.js nor Circle.js switch to great-circle interpolation (from flat/geodesic.js) when the view is in geographic mode, drawn shapes are distorted at high latitudes.
1.bug_scenario: When drawing circles, squares, boxes or other regular shapes in a view that has useGeographic enabled, the shapes come out warped at high latitudes.  A circle drawn by click-and-drag does not extend to the cursor, regular polygons (square, triangle, etc.) are no longer “regular,” and a box drawn with createBox is skewed unless the projection happens to be parallel to WGS84.  In non-geographic mode these shapes look correct.

2.explanation:
• src/ol/interaction/Draw.js contains the geometryFunction implementations for Circle, Square, Box and regular polygons. It computes center-to-pointer distances and vertex positions in simple map units, ignoring the view’s useGeographic (spherical) setting.
• src/ol/geom/Circle.js’s setCenterAndRadius method likewise lays out a Cartesian circle ring in flat coordinates, so geographic distortion isn’t handled.
• src/ol/geom/flat/geodesic.js already provides the necessary great-circle interpolation and offset routines. It needs to be wired into Draw.js (and possibly Circle.js) when useGeographic is set so that shapes are generated by geodesic distance rather than planar math.
2.bug_scenario: When drawing circles and regular polygons in “useGeographic” (spherical) mode, the shapes come out badly distorted. Circles don’t reach the cursor at high latitudes and regular polygons or boxes are no longer regular in view coordinates. The existing Draw interaction assumes a flat Cartesian canvas for computing radii and vertices, so geographic (“great-circle”) distance isn’t taken into account.
